prompt.context: Our client is a Canadian-based Timber Company in 2009. It primarily makes 2x4s, and the U.S. Residential construction market is, by far, the largest consumer of these products. It also sells sawdust, which is a derivative of 2x4 production. The housing crash has just happened, and demand has dropped precipitously. The client is in dire financial straits and bleeding cash.
prompt.question: What can we do to turn it around?

clarifying_info.a: It is privately owned; the family has cash to spend if it makes sense.

clarifying_info.q: What does the production process look like?
clarifying_info.a: Two-step process: trees are cut down, sent to a saw mill, then transported by truck to a distribution warehouse.

All equipment is brand new, employees are optimized, and the company is running at full capacity. Trucks are new and fuel-efficient (bought during boom times). The company is the leanest, most-efficient operation in the business.
The company holds one-third market share. The rest of the industry is small, fragmented, and much higher on the cost curve.
The company leases land for trees from the Canadian government and pays per tree cut down. Cost of that lease is negligible.
2x4s are sent by truck to the closest warehouse in Chicago, and then buyers purchase from there. It is a commodity market — all products are the same.

clarifying_info.q: Can we diversify into other revenue streams (e.g., engineered wood, furniture, pellets, etc.)?
clarifying_info.a: No. The firm is not set up to pursue other revenue streams and doing so would be prohibitively expensive.

exhibits.title: Interviewer Hint Sheet
exhibits.shows: A list of contextual facts the interviewer may reveal one at a time throughout the discussion — not a chart or table. Contains seven numbered pieces of information about company ownership, operations, cost position, market share, land lease, distribution, and revenue diversification constraints.
exhibits.data: (1) Privately owned, family has cash. (2) 2-step production: cut trees → saw mill → truck to warehouse. (3) Brand-new equipment, optimized staff, full capacity, fuel-efficient trucks — lowest-cost operator. (4) 1/3 market share; rest of industry small, fragmented, higher cost curve. (5) Leases land from Canadian government, pays per tree cut — negligible cost. (6) 2x4s trucked to Chicago warehouse; commodity market, products identical. (7) Other revenue streams not feasible — prohibitively expensive to pursue.

framework: Define the problem: demand collapse in a commodity market with no short-term demand lever
Assess cost position and operational efficiency: can costs be cut further?
Evaluate revenue side: alternative products or markets
Assess competitive dynamics: what happens to higher-cost competitors?
Consider strategic options: wait it out, consolidate, or exit
Evaluate financial runway: does the family's cash provide a bridge?

questions.prompt: Can the company cut costs to reduce cash burn?
questions.guidance: Strong answer recognizes the company is already the lowest-cost producer with brand-new equipment running at full capacity. There is no meaningful cost reduction available. Candidate should articulate this clearly after probing and not get stuck trying to find operational savings.

questions.prompt: Are there alternative revenue streams the company can pursue (e.g., engineered wood, wood pellets, furniture components, sawdust monetization)?
questions.guidance: Strong answer generates several creative ideas across the value chain and adjacent markets. However, the interviewer will shoot down each idea as not feasible given the firm's setup and the prohibitive cost of retooling. Candidate should accept the pushback calmly, continue ideating, and ultimately recognize that diversification is not a viable near-term option.

questions.prompt: Given that smaller competitors are higher on the cost curve, what happens to industry supply over time?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies that higher-cost competitors will fail first as prices fall. This will reduce industry supply, eventually rebalancing supply and demand and pushing prices back up. The client, as lowest-cost producer, is best positioned to survive and benefit.

questions.prompt: What strategic options does the client have?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers at least three options: (1) Liquidation — not optimal given cost leadership and market share, but not unreasonable; (2) Wait it out — smaller competitors will exit, supply will contract, prices will recover, and housing demand will recover with GDP growth (can reference 2009 stimulus); (3) Buy out smaller competitors using family cash to accelerate capacity reduction and improve pricing sooner. Candidate should flag antitrust risk on the acquisition option.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternative revenue streams or strategic moves might the company consider to weather the downturn?

categories.name: Geographic Diversification
ideas: Export to markets less affected by U.S. housing crash
Enter Asian or European construction markets

categories.name: Vertical Integration
ideas: Move downstream into prefab housing components
Partner with homebuilders for guaranteed offtake

categories.name: Consolidation / M&A
ideas: Acquire distressed smaller competitors to take capacity offline
Buy competitor assets at distressed prices to strengthen long-run position — note antitrust risk

categories.name: Financial / Structural
ideas: Use family cash as bridge financing to outlast competitors
Negotiate deferred payments on government tree leases

recommendation: Do not liquidate — the company is the lowest-cost producer with 1/3 market share and is best positioned to survive and dominate post-recovery
Wait out the downturn: higher-cost competitors will exit first, supply will contract, and prices will recover as housing tracks GDP growth
Selectively use the family's available capital to acquire distressed competitors and accelerate capacity reduction, improving the supply/demand balance sooner
risks: Antitrust scrutiny if acquisition of competitors is too aggressive
Duration risk — housing recovery may take longer than family cash can bridge
Demand may shift structurally (e.g., away from traditional wood-frame construction)
next_steps: Model cash burn rate vs. family cash reserves to determine financial runway
Identify which competitors are most distressed and assess acquisition targets
Monitor housing starts and GDP indicators for signs of demand recovery
Engage antitrust counsel before pursuing any competitor acquisitions
